Lower risk than the culture batches — these are grammar claims rather than claims about rooms — but three items want a native eye: the まえに-never-takes-past rule as stated absolutely, the ながら one-subject constraint, and the な-adjective exception list.

point.en: five ways to place two actions in time

exp.what: This step handed you five ways to say that one thing happened around another, and English covers all five with after, before and while. Japanese picks the form from where the join sits and from what shape the verb in front of it takes — so the choice has to be made before you can build the sentence, not after.
exp.build: 〜てから: after, and the second thing WAITS for the first. 〜たあとで: after, neutral about waiting. 〜まえに: before, and the verb in front is always dictionary form. 〜ながら: at the same time, one person, and the ながら half is the background action. 〜とき: the general wrapper — when, at the time of.
exp.when: Every account of a routine, a recipe, a journey or a day, which is exactly what this step's composition asks you for. It is also the machinery of every set of instructions you will ever read.
exp.watch: Two hard edges. まえに NEVER takes past tense — 寝るまえに, however long ago the sleeping was — because the まえ clause is measured against the main verb rather than against now. And ながら needs ONE person doing both actions; for two people the shape is 〜ている間に.

ex: ご飯を食べてから、出かけます。
After eating — and nothing happens until it's done.
寝るまえに、歯を磨きます。
音楽を聞きながら、勉強します。
While listening — one person, both actions.

seg: THE POINT — から makes it 'and only then'
the second action, which waits for the first
deep.note: まえに takes the DICTIONARY form no matter when it happened. The tense lives in the main clause, never in the まえ clause.

wr.t: まえに never takes the past. 寝たまえに is wrong however long ago the sleeping was, because the まえ clause is measured against the main verb rather than against now — the same relativity that puts the bag in a different city in 行くとき and 行ったとき.
wr.jp: 寝るまえに、歯を磨きました。
wr.en: I brushed my teeth before bed — past in the MAIN clause only.

wr.t: ながら needs one subject doing both actions. 音楽を聞きながら勉強します is you, twice over. Two different people take 〜ている間に instead, and using ながら there quietly claims you did both things yourself.
wr.jp: 母が寝ている間に、掃除しました。
wr.en: I cleaned while my mother slept — two people, so 間に.

drill.note: Pick the join from the relation: waiting, neutral order, before, simultaneous, or a general when.

items.q: ご飯を食べ___、出かけます。
items.en: Nothing happens until the eating is finished.
items.why: てから is the one that makes the second action wait.
まえに always takes the dictionary form.

items.q: 音楽を聞き___、勉強します。
items.en: Both at once, and both by you.
items.why: ながら — one person, two simultaneous actions.

items.q: 母が寝ている___、掃除しました。
items.why: ながら needs one subject; two people take 間に.

items.q: 日本に___とき、京都でかばんを買いました。
items.en: The bag came from Kyoto — so you had already arrived.
items.why: た + とき means after arriving. 行くとき would put the bag at the airport at home.

exp.what: Six lessons in this step rest on one fact nobody has stated as a system: every Japanese adjective belongs to one of two families, and which family it is in decides its past, its negative, its て-form, its adverb and its なる. This is not a spelling detail. They are two different machines wearing the same job.
exp.build: い-adjectives conjugate THEMSELVES: 高い → 高かった → 高くない → 高くて → 高く → 高くなる. な-adjectives never conjugate at all and です does the work: 静か → 静かでした → 静かではない → 静かで → 静かに → 静かになる. The な itself only surfaces in front of a noun — 静かな部屋.
exp.when: Every sentence with a description in it, which is most sentences you will ever build. Getting the family right is upstream of six separate patterns.
exp.watch: The commonest early error in the whole course is 高いでした. An い-adjective carries its own past, so です stays flat behind it: 高かったです. And きれい, 嫌い, 有名, 元気 all END in い and are な-adjectives — the い belongs to the root, not to the ending.

ex: この部屋は高かったです。
い-adjective: the word carries its own past, です stays flat.
この部屋は静かでした。
な-adjective: the word never moves, です carries everything.
きれい ends in い and takes な — the classic trap.

seg: THE POINT — the adjective conjugated ITSELF into the past
…and です stays flat. 高いでした is the error this prevents
deep.note: The な family is the exact mirror: the word never changes and です does all of the work.

wr.t: きれい, 嫌い, 有名, 元気 all end in い and are な-adjectives. The い belongs to the root rather than to the ending, which is why きれくない is broken and きれいではない is right. No rule predicts these — they are a short list, learned.
wr.en: A lovely room — な, in spite of the い.

wr.t: The adverb forms split the same way, and this is where the two machines are easiest to see side by side: い becomes く, な becomes に. Same job, different join, and the join is decided entirely by which family the word was in all along.
wr.jp: 静かに歩いてください。
wr.en: Please walk quietly — な takes に.

drill.note: Decide the family first. Everything else follows from it without a further choice.

items.why: い-adjectives carry their own past and です stays flat.
な-adjectives never conjugate; です does the tense.
きれい ends in い and is a な-adjective.
な-adjectives take に; い-adjectives take く.
An い-adjective already holds the past; です cannot hold it as well.
